segments.narration: In 1850, German inventor Wilhelm Bauer designed a revolutionary submarine to break a naval blockade.
He built the Brandtaucher, a revolutionary iron diving boat powered by a crew of three turning large tread wheels connected to a propeller.
During a public demonstration in Kiel harbor, the vessel simply vanished beneath the murky green waves. Did a structural weld crack, or did the air supply fail?
The heavy iron hull plunged straight to the seafloor after an equipment failure, trapping the crew as water pooled inside.

They survived by waiting hours for water to flood the interior, compressing the trapped air until the internal pressure finally matched the sea, letting them pop the hatch and swim up. How did they breathe while crushed in pitch-black mud?

accuracy_flags.claim: Every man inside the iron tube suffocated in total silence. In 1838, German inventor Wilhelm Bauer was obsessed with conquering the ocean depths.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference states the Brandtaucher was built in 1850 (not 1838), and Bauer and his two companions successfully escaped alive—they did not suffocate.

accuracy_flags.claim: Inventor Wilhelm Bauer built the Brandtaucher in 1838.
accuracy_flags.note: The Brandtaucher was built in 1850, not 1838. Also, the reference states it was propelled by a crew of three turning tread wheels connected to a propeller, not two men turning a paddle wheel.

accuracy_flags.claim: Water flooded the ballast tanks, instantly dragging the iron hull to the seabed.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference explicitly notes that enclosed ballast tanks were eliminated; instead, water pooled loosely in the bottom of the hull.
